title: Balabhadra Bhattacharya
html:
A Companion on the Road to Mathura

When Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu set out from Nilachala for Vrindavana through the forests of Jharikhanda, only one of His devotees went with Him as His companion — the Bengali brahmana Balabhadra Bhattacharya. He cooked the Lord's meals, collected alms for Him, guarded Him in the forest and in foreign lands, drew Him out of the waters of the Yamuna when the Lord plunged into them in ecstasy, and saw with his own eyes pastimes of which he would later tell the devotees in Puri. Krishnadasa Kaviraja counts him among the branches of the Chaitanya tree:

“Balabhadra Bhattacarya, a true devotee, served the Lord as His brahmacari on the journey to Mathura.” (CC, Adi 10.146)

In the “Charitamrita” he is called Balabhadra Bhattacharya, simply the Bhattacharya, or Balabhadra, and once Balabhadra Bhatta; the “Anubhashya,” too, heads this verse “Balabhadra Bhatta.” Kavi Karnapura in his drama “Chaitanya-chandrodaya” calls him Balabhadra-bhattacharya; Govinda-deva in the “Gaura-krishnodaya” calls him now the Bhatta, now Balabhadra Bhattacharya, now the Bhattacharya; and Murari Gupta calls him Baladeva.1

Why Balabhadra's service is called the service of a brahmachari, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati explains in his “Anubhashya” on this verse: a sannyasi does not cook or attend to other household matters — such services he accepts from householders; the sannyasi is the guru, and brahmacharis are his disciples. So on the road Balabhadra performed for the Lord the duties of a brahmachari. As acharya, the Lord kept the rules of sannyasa to teach the world; yet His measure was Vaishnavism, not birth, and we shall see that on the way He accepted invitations from great souls of the lower classes and ate food cooked by a Sanodiya brahmana, following the example of Madhavendra Puri.

Of his worldly life little is known. He was a brahmana, and Svarupa Damodara, proposing him to the Lord as a companion, said of him: “He is full of love for You, and he is learned, saintly and noble.” The Lord Himself acknowledged his learning: “You are a learned man,” He told him once in Vrindavana. He was a Bengali, a Gaudiya: the Pathans would call him and his servant “the Bengalis,” and Svarupa says that he came with the Lord from Gauda and wished to visit all the holy places. He had his own servant, also a brahmana, whose name the sources do not give; he carried the cloth and the waterpot. Neither Balabhadra's birthplace, nor his parents and disciples, nor the year and day of his appearance and departure are recorded; nor are his days found in the Vaishnava calendar of the Sri Chaitanya Saraswat Math.

Madhurekshana

Who he is in Krishna's eternal pastimes, Kavi Karnapura tells us:

“Balabhadra Bhattacharya is Sri Madhurekshana.” (“Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” 171)

The verse stands in the list of Srimati Radharani's friends that opens with Vishakha (verses 160–172), within the section of the “Gaura-ganoddesha-dipika” on the gopis, the “devotee's power” (verses 146–179). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta gives the same identity in his “Anubhashya” on CC, Adi 10.146: “Balabhadra Bhattacharya is Madhurekshana of Vraja.” Thus the Lord's companion on the forest roads is not merely a pious pandit from Bengal but one of Radha's eternal friends, who descended into Gaura's pastimes together with the Lord to serve Him here as well.

From Shantipura to Nilachala

The “Charitamrita” first names him on the Lord's return from Gauda. That year Mahaprabhu had set out from Nilachala for Vrindavana but went only as far as Kanai-natashala and turned back. At Shantipura, in the house of Advaita Acharya, He told the devotees He would take only two with Him to Nilachala, and would meet the rest at the Ratha-yatra:

“With two companions — Balabhadra Bhattacarya and Damodara Pandita — the Lord came to Nilacala.” (CC, Madhya 1.236)

Govinda-deva says the same: the Lord came to Jagannatha “with the Bhatta [Balabhadra], the Acharya, with the brahmin Damodara Pandita and with His servants” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 13.59). Svarupa would recall this later: Balabhadra “came with You from Gauda.”

The Choice of Svarupa and Ramananda

The next year, after the Ratha-yatra, when autumn came, the Lord resolved to go to Vrindavana. He consulted in private with Ramananda Raya and Svarupa Damodara: He would rise at night and go through the forest alone, taking no one with Him. His two intimate companions pleaded with Him for a long time, and at last they said:

“You are the independent Lord. Whatever You wish, You will do; You depend on no one. But hear one request from the two of us. You Yourself have said, ‘In your happiness is My happiness.’ Our hearts will be very happy, O merciful Lord, if You grant us one request. We must ask that one good brahmana go with You. He will collect alms and give You Your meals, and he will carry Your waterpot. On the forest path there is no brahmana whose food You could accept. Permit one brahmana to go with You.” (CC, Madhya 17.8–12)

The happiness of the devotees is the Lord's joy, and the Lord's joy is the devotees' happiness; so the Lord, who had wished to go alone, yielded to their request. He made only one condition: He would take none of His old companions, lest the others be unhappy — let it be someone new, “whose heart is full of love.” Then Svarupa said:

“Here is Balabhadra Bhattacarya. He is full of love for You, and he is learned, saintly and noble. He came with You from Gauda at the very start, and he wishes to visit all the holy places. With him is a brahmana servant, and on the road the Bhattacarya himself will serve You and see to Your meals. If You take him with You, everyone will be happy, and You will meet no hardship on the forest path. That brahmana will carry Your cloth and waterpot, and the Bhattacarya will go begging alms and give You Your meals.” The Lord accepted Svarupa's words and took Balabhadra Bhattacarya with Him. (CC, Madhya 17.15–20)

So the Lord's two closest companions entrusted the Lord Himself to Balabhadra: His care on the road, His meals, His peace and safety in the forest. One of the biographies says that Ramananda and Svarupa gave the Lord two companions — Balabhadra and a brahmana servant besides; but the “Charitamrita,” in its summary of the pastimes, says that “only Balabhadra Bhattacarya stayed with Him” (Madhya 1.238), and the biographies, too, call him the Lord's “only companion.”2 In the evening the Lord received Jagannatha's permission, and at the end of the night He set out in secret, and Balabhadra went with Him; Govinda-deva writes that the Lord left “secretly … at night, together with Balabhadra Bhattacharya” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.2).

Jharikhanda

The Lord went through the lonely forests of Jharikhanda chanting Krishna's name. Tigers, elephants, rhinoceroses and boars, herd upon herd, crossed His path, and absorbed in ecstasy He walked straight through their midst:

“Seeing this, the Bhattacarya was terrified, but by the Lord's power the animals stood aside.” (CC, Madhya 17.27)

The companion's fear here is no weakness to be smiled at: it sets off the Lord's fearlessness and power. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta remarks that a maha-bhagavata, absorbed in love for Krishna, knows no fear — and such is the Lord on this forest road; while a Bengali pandit in the wild forests of a foreign land plays in His pastime a role natural to him, and it is through his eyes that we see what followed. A tiger touched by the Lord's foot sprang up and danced, crying “Krishna!”; maddened elephants, sprinkled with water by the Lord, began to sing and dance —

“Some fell to the ground, and some trumpeted loudly. Seeing this, the Bhattacarya was struck with wonder.” (CC, Madhya 17.33)

Does and five or seven tigers walked together behind the Lord and danced —

“The tigers danced and wept together with the does, and Balabhadra Bhattacarya watched, amazed at this wondrous play.” (CC, Madhya 17.41)

Every forest seemed to the Lord to be Vrindavana:

“Seeing a forest, He would take it for Vrndavana; seeing a hill, He would think it Govardhana. Wherever He saw a river, He took it for the Kalindi. Overwhelmed by love, the Lord danced and fell down weeping.” (CC, Madhya 17.55–56)

Balabhadra meanwhile served. Along the road he gathered greens, roots and fruits. In every village five or seven brahmanas would invite the Lord, and people brought Balabhadra grain, milk, yogurt, ghee and sugar — everyone served the Lord as he could.3 Where there were no brahmanas, the Lord and His companion were invited by great souls of the lower classes: Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains that these were shudra mahajanas, brahmanas by initiation, for the Lord looked at Vaishnavism, not at birth. From the vegetables gathered in the forest Balabhadra cooked dishes the Lord loved, and for the empty stretches, where for days there was no dwelling, he kept with him grain for two or four days. The Lord was perfectly content with the simple forest fare, and happier still with the solitude.

“The Bhattacarya served Him lovingly, like a servant, and his brahmana carried the waterpot and the outer cloth.” (CC, Madhya 17.65)

Once the Lord spoke to him of His earlier journey — how He had set out for Vrindavana through Gauda and turned back halfway: there had been crowds all around, but now, in the forest, no trouble had come to Him — by Krishna's mercy He was very happy. And embracing the Bhattacharya, He said:

“By your kindness I have found so much happiness.” He replied, “You are Krsna! You are merciful! I am a fallen soul, yet You have been kind to me. I am worthless, yet You have brought me with You. In Your mercy, my Lord, You have taken Your meals from my hand. You have made a lowly crow equal to Garuda. You are the independent Lord, Svayam Bhagavan Himself.” (CC, Madhya 17.76–79)

The words “You are Krishna” are neither flattery nor exaggeration: Balabhadra knows that his Lord is Krishna Himself, and so he sees a miracle of mercy in His eating from his hands. And he recited a verse of Sridhara Svami:

“I bow down to Madhava, the supreme bliss, whose mercy makes the mute eloquent and lets the lame cross a mountain.” (CC, Madhya 17.80; “Bhavartha-dipika” 1.1.1)

“In this way Balabhadra offered praise, and by his loving service he pleased the Lord.” (CC, Madhya 17.81)

So in one conversation both are revealed: the Lord is grateful for loving service and Himself ascribes His happiness to His servant's kindness, while the servant, seeing Krishna in Him, counts himself as nothing and cannot cease to marvel at His mercy.

Kashi, Prayaga, Mathura

In Kashi the Lord was met by Tapana Mishra. Govinda-deva writes that he saw the Lord from afar “with Balabhadra” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.10). The “Charitamrita” relates:

“With all his family he drank the water that had washed the Lord's feet, and he honoured the Bhattacarya with worship. He invited the Lord and fed Him in his home, having Balabhadra Bhattacarya do the cooking.” (CC, Madhya 17.88–89)

Tapana Mishra quickly made everything ready for cooking, and in his house Balabhadra cooked for the Lord; after the meal the Lord's feet were massaged by the boy Raghunatha, the future Raghunatha Bhatta Gosvami.

From Kashi the road led through Prayaga. There, the moment He saw the Yamuna, the Lord leapt into it in love, and Balabhadra hurriedly caught hold of Him and lifted Him out (CC, Madhya 17.150). The Lord was not drowning as a man of this world drowns: He plunged into the Yamuna overwhelmed by prema, and Balabhadra's service was care for the Lord absorbed in ecstasy. So it would be again later.

In Mathura the Lord was approached by a Sanodiya brahmana, a disciple of Madhavendra Puri. Seeing His love, he guessed that the Lord was connected with Madhavendra: “Love for Krsna is found where there is a connection with him.”

“Then the Bhattacarya told him of the connection, and hearing it the brahmana began to dance with joy.” (CC, Madhya 17.174)

The brahmana took the Lord to his home and asked Balabhadra to cook His meal. But the Lord smiled and said: “Puri Gosani has taken his meals in your house. You yourself give Me My meal” (CC, Madhya 17.176–177). Sanodiya brahmanas were regarded as a community in whose houses sannyasis do not eat; but Madhavendra Puri, seeing this brahmana's Vaishnava conduct, made him his disciple and ate with him — and the Lord followed the conduct of His great predecessor.4

From then on the Sanodiya brahmana was the Lord's guide through the twelve forests of Vraja, and together with Balabhadra he guarded Him. Once the Lord, seeing the necks of peacocks that reminded Him of Krishna, fell unconscious.

“Seeing the Lord unconscious, the brahmana and the Bhattacarya tried to revive Him. Hurriedly they took Mahaprabhu's outer cloth, sprinkled His body with water and fanned Him with the cloth. They spoke the name of Krsna loudly in the Lord's ear, and regaining consciousness, the Lord rolled about on the ground. In that forest, impassable with thorns, His body was scratched and cut. The Bhattacarya took the Lord on his lap and calmed Him. In His absorption in Krsna the Lord's mind was overwhelmed with love. Crying ‘Say it! Say it!’ He got up and began to dance. The Bhattacarya and the brahmana sang the name of Krsna, and the Lord went on along the path, dancing all the way.” (CC, Madhya 17.219–224)

Govinda-deva tells of a similar moment: after the conversation of the parrots the Lord fell down “as if lifeless,” and “the Bhattacharya soon brought Him back to consciousness” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.27–28). At Radha-kunda the Lord marked Himself with tilaka of clay from its bank and with Balabhadra's help took some of the clay along; at Brahma-kunda the Bhattacharya cooked, and the Lord ate after bathing there (CC, Madhya 18.14, 18.21).

Kaliya's Lake

Once word went round Vrindavana that Krishna was again to be seen at Kaliya's lake: at night people saw Him dancing on the serpent Kaliya, with jewels flashing on the serpent's hoods. Guileless Balabhadra believed it, and in the evening he wished to go and see.

“Then the Bhattacarya said at the Lord's feet, ‘Give me permission, and I shall go and have darsana of Krsna!’ At this the Lord gave him a slap and said, ‘You are a learned man, yet you have become a fool by listening to the words of fools. Why would Krsna give darsana in the age of Kali? Foolish people are making an uproar out of their own delusion. Do not go mad. Stay at home and sit quietly. You can go tomorrow night and have darsana of Krsna.’” (CC, Madhya 18.99–102)

In the morning everything came to light: respectable people told the Lord that at night a fisherman fished from a boat with a lamp on the lake, and from afar people took the boat for Kaliya, the lamp for his jewels and the fisherman for Krishna Himself (CC, Madhya 18.103–106). Balabhadra's delusion was dispelled.5

This episode is not the story of a credulous man but a lesson for everyone. The Lord's slap is a teacher's caress: He corrects His servant, and with him the whole world. In the age of Kali Krishna does not show Himself to people in that way, for display, and to ascribe Krishna's position to an ordinary jiva is an offence; the Lord says this here too, in the same chapter of the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 18.111–116). Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, in his chapter heading at Madhya 17.16, writes of Balabhadra that a guileless brahmana in whom the tendency to fruitive work was still strong was given the chance to be purified in the Lord's company. This is a lesson in the power of the Lord's company: whomever He draws close, He leads to pure devotion. And who Balabhadra is in the eternal pastimes we already know from Karnapura: Madhurekshana, Radha's friend — and so we must not see in him a worldly man.

Leaving Vraja

The Lord stayed at Akrura-tirtha, and all Mathura longed to invite Him.

“All the people of Mathura — brahmanas and respectable folk — came to the Bhattacarya to invite the Lord. In a single day ten or twenty invitations would come, but the Bhattacarya would accept only one.” (CC, Madhya 18.130–131)

One day the Lord, sitting on the ghata of Akrura-tirtha, remembered that here Akrura had seen Vaikuntha and the people of Vraja had seen Goloka, and He threw Himself into the Yamuna:

“With these words He leapt into the water and stayed submerged beneath it. Seeing this, Krsnadasa wept and cried out, and the Bhattacarya quickly came and pulled the Lord out.” (CC, Madhya 18.137–138)

Govinda-deva gives the Bhattacharya's thought at that moment as well: “Alas, what would have happened had I not been here?” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.52).

Svarupa and Ramananda had entrusted the Lord to Balabhadra so that no harm should come to Him on the road. And now, anxious for the Lord, absorbed in prema and surrounded by crowds, he took counsel in private with his elder — the Sanodiya brahmana, the disciple of Madhavendra Puri:

“Today I was here, and I pulled the Lord out. But if He dives in at Vrndavana, who will pull Him out? The crowds of people, the bother of invitations, the Lord's constant absorption — none of this seems good to me. If we take the Lord away from Vrndavana, all will be well. This is a good plan.” (CC, Madhya 18.140–142)

The brahmana proposed going to Prayaga by the road along the Ganga, through Soro-kshetra: the month of Magha had begun, and they would be in time for the bathing during Makara-sankranti.6 He advised Balabhadra to tell the Lord what troubled him. Balabhadra did so: he told the Lord he could no longer bear the crowds and would be happy to reach Prayaga in time (CC, Madhya 18.143–151).

This decision was born of love: neither Svarupa nor Ramananda had told Balabhadra to take the Lord away from Vraja in particular — he was moved by a servant's anxiety for the Lord entrusted to his care, and he took counsel with his elder, the disciple of Madhavendra. And the Lord agreed for His devotee's sake:

“Although the Lord had no wish to leave Vrndavana, to fulfil His devotee's wish He spoke sweet words: ‘You brought Me here and showed Me Vrndavana. I shall never be able to repay this debt. Whatever you wish, that I will do. Wherever you take Me, there I will go.’” (CC, Madhya 18.152–154)

The Lord calls Himself His servant's debtor — so highly does He value his love. The summary of the pastimes says the same briefly: seeing the places of the pastimes, the Lord became overwhelmed with love, “and Balabhadra led Him away from Mathura” (CC, Madhya 1.240); then, by the road along the Ganga, he brought the Lord to Prayaga (Madhya 1.241). Karnapura writes that the pious Balabhadra-bhattacharya and others, seeing the Lord senseless from excess of love, thought, “Ah, misfortune has come!” — “and as if by force led the Lord away from Vrindavana”; and Sarvabhauma in his drama says that the Lord was “as if drawn to Himself by Jagannatha, who could not bear separation from Him” (“Chaitanya-chandrodaya,” Act 9). In Govinda-deva the Lord leaves “in order to deliver Sanatana and others” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.59). The Lord's will is fulfilled through His servant's love.7

Next morning, after His bath, the Lord was overcome with love at the thought that He was leaving Vrindavana, though outwardly He did not show it. Understanding His state, Balabhadra proposed going to Mahavana, that is, Gokula, and they crossed the Yamuna by boat (CC, Madhya 18.155–157).

The Pathans

On the way the Lord stopped to rest beneath a tree. Cows were grazing nearby; a cowherd boy began to play his flute, and at that sound the Lord fell unconscious, foam on His lips. Just then ten Pathan horsemen rode up. Thinking that the four companions had drugged the monk and robbed Him, they seized them and meant to put them to death.

“Then the Pathans bound the four men and wanted to cut them down. The Bengalis all began to tremble. Krsnadasa was a Rajput and utterly fearless. That brahmana too was fearless, and very bold of speech.” (CC, Madhya 18.166–167)

The Bengalis were Balabhadra and his servant; and the soldiers said as much: “You two are men of the west, from Mathura, and these two Bengali cheats are trembling” (CC, Madhya 18.172). The men of that country, the Sanodiya brahmana and Krishnadasa the Rajput, answered the Pathans boldly, while for a Bengali brahmana in a foreign land fear was natural — and all the brighter is what followed. The Lord came to Himself with a thunderous cry of “Hari! Hari!”, rose and danced, and that sound pierced the soldiers' hearts like the point of a spear; they let the captives go.

“The Bhattacarya came, took hold of the Lord and seated Him. Seeing the mlecchas, Mahaprabhu returned to outward consciousness.” (CC, Madhya 18.180)

The soldiers began telling the Lord that these four were robbers, but He replied:

“They are not cheats; they are My companions. I am a mendicant sannyasi and have no wealth at all. Because of the falling sickness I sometimes lose consciousness, and these four kindly look after Me.” (CC, Madhya 18.183–184)

So the Lord spoke of Himself before strangers, concealing His prema: His unconsciousness is no illness but the highest state of divine love, which He did not disclose to those who could not understand it.

Later, when the Lord wished to send the Sanodiya brahmana and Krishnadasa home, they asked to go with Him as far as Prayaga: “This is a land of mlecchas, and someone somewhere may make trouble. The Bhattacarya is a scholar; he does not know how to talk to them” (CC, Madhya 18.217).8 The Lord smiled, and they went on with Him.

Prayaga, Adaila, Kashi

The Lord reached Prayaga during the ten days of bathing at the Triveni, when the sun enters Makara. Here Sri Rupa and his younger brother Vallabha (Anupama) came to Him. When a brahmana invited the Lord to a meal,

“The Bhattacarya invited the two brothers as well, and they received the plate with the remnants of the Lord's prasada.” (CC, Madhya 19.59)9

Then Vallabha Bhatta took the Lord by boat across the Yamuna to Adaila; in the boat were Rupa, Anupama, Balabhadra and Krishnadasa the Rajput. When at the Triveni the Lord, seeing the dark waters of the Yamuna, leapt into the river with a loud cry, all who were in the boat hurriedly caught hold of Him and drew Him out, and He danced in the boat (CC, Madhya 19.79–80). In his house Vallabha worshipped the Lord,

“…and with due respect he had Balabhadra Bhattacarya do the cooking.” (CC, Madhya 19.87)

And afterwards “the Bhattacarya had the Lord's remnants given to Sri Rupa, and Krsnadasa then received what remained of that prasada” (CC, Madhya 19.89). Govinda-deva writes that the Lord, having shown mercy to Rupa and Vallabha, introduced them “to the Bhatta and other devotees” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.70) — apparently to Balabhadra.

On the way back, in Kashi, Balabhadra remained with the Lord all the while as His companion; Chandrashekhara, in whose house the Lord stayed, invited the Bhattacharya too to a meal (CC, Madhya 19.248).

Back to Nilachala

From Kashi the Lord returned to Puri the same way — through the forests of Jharikhanda:

“Happily the Lord journeyed on with Balabhadra and, as before, sported in many ways with the deer and other creatures. Coming to Atharanala, He sent the brahmana Bhattacarya ahead to call His devotees.” (CC, Madhya 25.216–217)

So, at the Lord's word, Balabhadra was the first to bring Nilachala the news of His return. In Puri he became the witness whom others asked about the journey. Haridasa Thakura, glorifying the power of loud sankirtana, said to the Lord:

“Balabhadra Bhattacarya has told me how You did this in Jharikhanda on Your way to Vrndavana.” (CC, Antya 3.72)

This was the news that by the Lord's sankirtana the trees, beasts and birds of the Jharikhanda forests had attained liberation. Through the Lord and His companions, by the chain of hearing and chanting, everyone on His path became a Vaishnava, even those farthest from Krishna — and Balabhadra's accounts of Jharikhanda remained a testimony to that power.

And when the next year, after the Dola-yatra, Sanatana Gosvami prepared to go to Vrindavana by the forest road the Lord had taken,

“From Balabhadra Bhatta he wrote down everything: by which path, past which villages, rivers and hills the Lord went, and which pastime took place where.” (CC, Antya 4.210)

So even then Balabhadra was living in Puri with the Lord. The sources say nothing more of him.

In Other Original Sources

Murari Gupta, describing the Lord's journey to Vrindavana, says: “The Lord ran on, full of longing, like a maddened lion, and His companions, Baladeva and the others, devotedly ran after Him” (Murari Gupta's “Karcha,” 4.1.11); Baladeva here is our Balabhadra. Govinda-deva writes that the Lord left Mathura with five companions — three followers from Gauda and two devotees from Mathura (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.57); the “Charitamrita” names two from Gauda — Balabhadra and his servant.

One of the biographies says that Lochana Dasa too, in the “Chaitanya-mangala,” tells how the Lord wandered with Balabhadra Bhattacharya by the Yamuna and through Vrindavana's twelve forests.10

Narahari Chakravarti, in the “Namamrita-samudra,” where his prayers call upon the Lord's associates, turns to him as well:

“Balabhadra Bhattacharya! This is my prayer: may my mind abide in singing the qualities of Gaurachandra.” (“Namamrita-samudra” 96)

Significance

Balabhadra Bhattacharya's life, as the sources know it, is above all a long road at the Lord's side. Yet that road holds what Krishnadasa Kaviraja expressed in a single verse: a true devotee who served the Lord as His brahmachari. Svarupa and Ramananda chose him for his love; the Lord, who had wished to go alone, took him along for the devotees' happiness — and told him, “By your kindness I have found so much happiness,” and later, “I shall never be able to repay this debt.”

Balabhadra, for his part, saw in his Lord Krishna Himself, and in himself a lowly crow whom mercy had made equal to Garuda. His service was simple: to gather greens in the forest, to cook, to carry a store of grain, to draw the Lord out of the Yamuna, to take Him, scratched by thorns, on his lap, to lead Him away from danger. But with such simple service the eternal Madhurekshana, Radha's friend, served Gaura — and the Lord accepted it with gratitude.

And he remained the keeper of that journey's pastimes. From him Haridasa Thakura learned how the forests of Jharikhanda sang Krishna's name, and Sanatana Gosvami wrote down through which villages, by which rivers and hills the Lord had gone — so as to walk the same road. Thus his memory preserved Mahaprabhu's path for the Vaishnavas.

Notes

  1. One of the biographies once calls him Baladeva Bhattacharya; Murari Gupta, too, calls him Baladeva (“Karcha,” 4.1.11). This is he, and not Balarama or Nityananda, who are also called Balabhadra and Baladeva. Nor should he be confused with his namesakes — Balabhadra Acharya of Gopala Bhatta's circle, Balabhadra the disciple of Shyamananda, and others.
  2. There is no contradiction: the brahmana servant attended Balabhadra and was not the Lord's companion; so in the “Charitamrita” Svarupa speaks of him as Balabhadra's servant (Madhya 17.17). Govinda-deva counts three followers from Gauda when the Lord left Mathura (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.57); we follow the “Charitamrita.”
  3. One of the biographies says “five or seven people”; the “Charitamrita” says “five or seven brahmanas” (Madhya 17.58).
  4. One of the biographies, in its chapter on Balabhadra, writes that at the Sanodiya brahmana's house the Lord had Balabhadra cook. This differs from the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 17.176–181), where the Lord told the brahmana himself to cook — and from the same biography's chapter on the Sanodiya brahmana. We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  5. One of the biographies adds that Balabhadra, falling at the Lord's feet, asked His pardon; the “Charitamrita” (Madhya 18.103–106) does not say this. On the other hand, that account omits the slap and the words “you can go tomorrow night.”
  6. The sources differ on the time of the bathing. In the “Charitamrita” the month of Magha has already begun, and the days of Makara and the full moon lie ahead (Madhya 18.145–146); according to one biography, it is the bathing at the end of Magha, at Makara-sankranti; according to another, it was Magha and Makara-sankranti had already passed. Govinda-deva: “let us bathe at Prayaga when the sun is in Makara — there, where once the feet of Sri Guru, the lord of Puris, rested for several days” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.54). We follow the “Charitamrita.”
  7. The biographies tell this differently. According to one, the decision to lead the Lord away was taken by three — the Sanodiya brahmana, Balabhadra and Krishnadasa the Rajput — because of the excessive crowds, and the Lord agreed at the devotees' wish; according to another, the Lord could not refuse the Sanodiya brahmana, the revered godbrother of His guru. In Govinda-deva the Lord agreed “considering the time” (“Gaura-krishnodaya” 14.55). We follow the “Charitamrita”: Balabhadra and the Sanodiya brahmana took counsel together, and the Lord agreed to fulfil His devotee's wish (Madhya 18.139–154).
  8. Literally the Bengali verse says: “The Bhattacharya is a pandit; he does not know how to speak [with them]” (bhattacharya — pandita, kahite na janena bat). One of the biographies renders it just so: as a scholar, the Bhattacharya would not know what to say in such a situation; others say “he does not know the language.”
  9. The “Bhattacharya” here is Balabhadra, the Lord's companion, as Srila Bhaktisiddhanta explains in the “Anubhashya”; so too in Madhya 19.89. One of the biographies says plainly that in Prayaga Balabhadra invited Rupa and Vallabha and served them the remnants of the Lord's meal.
  10. In our text of Lochana Dasa's “Chaitanya-mangala” Balabhadra is not named at this point: the Lord's companion in Vraja there is the brahmana Krishnadasa.
